title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: a night-shift nurse walks out into a sky going pink. The Rig Veda sings to that light by name: Ushas, the dawn

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: Vasishtha asked Varuna, what did I do, and named drink, anger and dice out loud.

The hospital doors slide open and a nurse steps out after a long night shift. Her feet hurt. Her head is full of beeping. Then she looks up. The sky over the parking lot is going from gray to rose to gold, and for a second she forgets everything else. The birds have started. A bus hisses at the corner. Plenty of mornings like this go by unseen. The Rig Veda's poets turned to that light, gave it a name, and sang to it. Today, Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `OUT OF THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `GRAY, ROSE, GOLD.` → `THE POETS SANG TO IT.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, Ushas is a goddess, pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, driving away the dark. One hymn to her begins, in paraphrase: this light has come, the fairest of lights. Her bright sign is born. Then the poet notices time. The night has made room for the dawn, like a sister giving way to her sister. And then this line. Gone are the mortals who watched the earlier dawns. Now she is seen by us. And coming are those who will see her in mornings still ahead. Three groups of people under one light: those before us, us, and those after. Every sunrise, on this reading, joins them. The same hymn ends by waking everyone up. Rise, it says. The breath of life has come back to us. The dark has gone away. Light is coming near. She has opened a path for the sun to travel. The hymn holds two things together: one life is short, and the light it's lived under is shared. And the dawn isn't new each day. She is ancient and young at once, the hymn says, coming again and again.
screen: `USHAS: THE DAWN, A GODDESS.` · `THE FAIREST OF LIGHTS HAS COME.` · `THOSE BEFORE, US, THOSE AFTER.` · `RISE: THE BREATH HAS COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Turn toward a window if you can, or call a dawn you remember to mind, and feel the light on your face, real or remembered. Hold three people in that same light: someone before you who saw this sky and is gone, someone with you now, someone who will see it after you; if you pray, you can greet the morning in your own way.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns that sing to Ushas, the dawn, fairest of lights, seen by those before us, by us, and by those still to come.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. The dawn is ancient and young at once. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Hindu practice, dawn is often a time of prayer: bathing, chanting, and offering water to the rising sun, and the hymns to Ushas are part of the Rig Veda's recited text.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.113.1–3 (this light has come, fairest of lights; night has yielded to dawn, sister to sister)
Rig Veda 1.113.11 (gone are the mortals who saw the earlier dawn; now she is seen by us; coming are those who will see her later)
Rig Veda 1.113.13, 1.113.16 (ancient and ever young; rise, the breath of life has come to us, darkness has gone, light approaches, she has opened a path for the sun)

notes: Rig Veda 1.113 paraphrased throughout (no PD translation on the validator list). Confirm verse numbers, especially 1.113.13 (ancient, ever young) and 1.113.16 (rise, the breath of life).
'The fairest of lights' is the hymn's own superlative (1.113.1).
Ushas pictured as a young woman in bright clothes is a standard summary of her hymns, not a quotation. Confirm.
Kutsa as the seer of 1.113 (trapdoor) is from the tradition's index; confirm.
howItsDone mentions offering water to the rising sun (arghya, often with the Gayatri); confirm.
